content: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is a metabolic disorder caused by a deficiency in the liver enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH). This enzyme is essential for converting the amino acid phenylalanine into another amino acid, tyrosine. When PAH is deficient, phenylalanine accumulates in the body, leading to persistently elevated levels that progressively damage the central nervous system. If left untreated, children with PKU may experience seizures, intellectual disabilities, and microcephaly (a condition characterized by a smaller-than-normal head size). Additionally, reduced melanin production due to impaired tyrosine synthesis can result in decreased pigmentation, often presenting as a child with blonde hair and blue eyes. PKU is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. The prevalence of PKU varies across populations. In European, Chinese, and Korean populations, the birth prevalence is approximately 1 in 10,000 live births. In South-East England, the prevalence differs by ethnicity, with rates of 1.14 per 10,000 among white individuals, 0.11 per 10,000 among black individuals, and 0.29 per 10,000 among Asian individuals. In India, the prevalence is estimated at 0.5 per 10,000 live births. Globally, the incidence of PKU shows significant variability, with Turkey having the highest reported rates (1 in 2,600) and Finland and Japan having the lowest (1 in 200,000 and 1 in 125,000, respectively). PKU is considered a treatable condition and is included in many newborn screening programs worldwide. The standard treatment involves a phenylalanine-restricted diet, achieved through a low-protein diet supplemented with a synthetic protein substitute. Blood phenylalanine levels are regularly monitored, and dietary adjustments are made as needed. National and international guidelines define safe phenylalanine levels, which vary by age and country. Strict dietary adherence is particularly critical during the first five years of life to ensure normal brain development. However, adherence often declines with age, potentially leading to reduced cognitive and executive function. In pregnant women with poorly controlled PKU, there is an increased risk of adverse fetal outcomes. Large neutral amino acids (LNAAs) include tyrosine, tryptophan, threonine, methionine, valine, isoleucine, leucine, histidine, and phenylalanine. This review focuses on the use of phenylalanine-free LNAA protein substitutes for managing PKU in individuals aged 12 years and older as an alternative to standard PKU protein substitutes. LNAAs are not recommended for children under 12 years of age due to insufficient evidence regarding their safety and efficacy in this age group. During early childhood, strict dietary control is essential to ensure normal neurological development. The rationale for using LNAA supplementation is based on the shared transport system for all LNAAs across the blood-brain barrier. By providing high concentrations of all LNAAs except phenylalanine, the transport of phenylalanine into the brain is competitively inhibited. This reduces phenylalanine levels in the brain, potentially mitigating its neurotoxic effects. LNAA transport occurs at both the gut-blood barrier and the blood-brain barrier. Phenylalanine-free LNAA supplementation can reduce phenylalanine absorption from the gut into the bloodstream and subsequently from the bloodstream into the brain, thereby lowering cerebral phenylalanine concentrations. Although PKU is a rare condition, it is one of the more common inborn errors of metabolism. If untreated during the first five years of life, it can lead to significant neurological and cognitive impairments. In later life, treatment aims to support healthy pregnancies in affected women and maintain adequate cognitive and executive function. The PKU diet can be challenging to follow, and this review seeks to determine whether LNAA supplementation can alleviate the dietary burden or serve as an alternative to standard PKU protein substitutes.
